strengths: The paper addresses an important issue for multilingual NLP: whether Wikipedia merits its widespread use as a high-quality pretraining resource. The reported duplication rates provide useful evidence of corpus redundancy, including substantial near-duplication across non-English editions.

The experimental coverage is substantial: monolingual pretraining across 51 languages, XLM-R language adaptation, and four reported downstream benchmarks. Comparisons between primary filtering, heuristic filtering, and approximately equal-character partitions provide several perspectives on data selection.

The analysis acknowledges heterogeneous outcomes and documents informative failures, particularly script filtering harming Moroccan Arabic sentiment analysis. These observations support the recommendation to consider language and task when choosing filters.
The linked implementation, architecture and training configurations in Appendix A, and detailed per-language results provide a useful foundation for reuse and further investigation.
weaknesses: The proposed quality tiers lack independent validation. Clustering languages by the proportions of articles and characters removed establishes susceptibility to the chosen filters, but does not establish linguistic quality or usefulness for pretraining. Short articles, templated articles, and foreign-script spans can contain useful information. Script filtering also misses contamination written in the same script, as acknowledged. A representative human audit of retained and removed material, or a narrower interpretation of the tiers, is needed to support the central quality claims.

The experiments do not isolate a quality-specific advantage over simply using less data. There is no size-matched random-pruning baseline, and comparable performance from both high- and low-scoring halves is consistent with redundancy or task saturation. Appendix A additionally changes tokenizers between raw and filtered DeBERTa conditions, while fixed epoch counts change optimization budgets as datasets shrink. Fixed-epoch pruning plausibly saves training work, but retained token counts, actual training costs, and filtering overhead are not reported. These limitations weaken the claims that quality outweighs quantity and enables resource-efficient training.

The inference supporting performance preservation is statistically invalid. Section 6.1 treats a nonsignificant Spearman correlation between removal amount and performance change as evidence of no significant performance decrease. That correlation does not test whether filtering causes an average loss or satisfies a noninferiority criterion. Material individual losses also occur: Table 5 reports Acehnese falling from 0.27 to 0.15 after primary filtering and Minangkabau from 0.65 to 0.53 after heuristic filtering. Paired effect estimates and uncertainty intervals are needed, with conclusions qualified by language and task.

The numerical reporting requires verification. The displayed Tier 4 rows in Table 6 average to approximately 0.63/0.60/0.62/0.61 for baseline/raw/primary/heuristic, whereas the reported averages are 0.59/0.66/0.66/0.65. This reverses the apparent average benefit of adaptation. Moreover, raw_wiki and +heuristic uncertainty values are identical in every language row across Tables 2–6, covering 118 rows. This pattern needs checking against the underlying run-level results before the reported uncertainty can be trusted.

Important reproducibility and clarity details remain unspecified in the manuscript: the Wikipedia snapshot and extraction procedure, MinHash configuration, KDE kernel/bandwidth and combination of filtering thresholds, validation split construction, and whether the five repetitions include pretraining randomness. Evaluation metrics also need explicit definitions; Figure 6 labels NER performance as accuracy, and the announced MasakhaPOS evaluation has no reported results. The code link is helpful, but versioned data and experiment configurations are needed. Together with the methodological and reporting issues above, these gaps warrant revision before a Findings recommendation.
